lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you met jobs in four sectors. Which sector is a nurse's job in? (Tertiary: services.) Today: skills, interests and pathways into jobs, and why any job is open to anyone.

A career is the path of work through your life. Most people change jobs, and many change careers, several times. Good choices start with knowing yourself: your interests (what you enjoy), your skills (what you can do) and your values (what matters to you).

One way to think about jobs: do you most enjoy working with people, with things and tools, or with ideas and data? A teacher works with people, an electrician with tools and a scientist with ideas. Many jobs mix all three.

Skills almost every job needs: communication, teamwork, solving problems, being reliable, using numbers and digital tools, and learning new things. You build them at school, in clubs and hobbies, in games with friends, and by volunteering.

Pathways: after school, some people go to college or sixth form, then university; others start an apprenticeship, earning a wage while learning on the job; others train in a trade or start their own business. Most jobs have more than one route.

No job is only for boys or only for girls. In 1865 Elizabeth Garrett Anderson became the first woman to qualify as a doctor in Britain. Katherine Johnson's mathematics helped send astronauts into space. Men are nurses; women are engineers and pilots.

Jobs change as the world changes. New ones appear, such as wind turbine technician or app designer; others change or vanish. So a love of learning matters as much as any one skill. Pay depends on skills, training and how much the work is needed.
Try it in the world: run a jobs fair in your village: build stalls for three different jobs, each with a sign saying the skills it needs and one way to train for it. Next: start a small business.

exercises.hint: You work and learn at the same time.
choices: learning a job while earning a wage
exercises.explain: Learning a job on the job, while earning a wage.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is an interest?
exercises.hint: Interests are about what you like.
exercises.explain: Something you enjoy doing, such as building or helping people.

exercises.prompt: Some jobs are only for boys.
exercises.hint: Think of Elizabeth Garrett Anderson and Katherine Johnson.
exercises.explain: False: every job is open to anyone who learns its skills.

exercises.prompt: Which job is mostly working with things and tools?
exercises.explain: An electrician wires houses: work with things and tools. Any job is open to anyone who learns its skills.

exercises.prompt: Which skill does almost every job need?
exercises.hint: Every job involves working with other people.
exercises.explain: Communication: listening, speaking and writing clearly.

exercises.prompt: Sort these jobs by what they mostly work with.
exercises.hint: Think about what fills most of the working day.
exercises.explain: People: nurse, care worker. Things and tools: mechanic, carpenter. Ideas and data: scientist, programmer.

exercises.prompt: Match each job to its work.
exercises.explain: Nurse: patients. Electrician: wiring. Programmer: code. Accountant: money.

exercises.prompt: Elizabeth Garrett Anderson was born in 1836 and qualified as a doctor in 1865. How old was she then, about?
exercises.hint: Take the birth year from the year she qualified.

exercises.prompt: Mimi loves puzzles with numbers and facts. Which job might suit her?
exercises.hint: Which job works with ideas and data?
exercises.explain: A data analyst works with numbers and facts every day.

exercises.prompt: Most people have the same job all their working life.
exercises.explain: False: most people change jobs, and many change careers, several times.

exercises.prompt: Why does a love of learning matter for a career?
exercises.hint: Think of jobs that did not exist 30 years ago.
choices: jobs change and new ones appear
exercises.explain: Jobs keep changing, so people who keep learning can move into new work.

exercises.prompt: Bram wants to earn while he trains to be an electrician. Which pathway fits?
exercises.explain: An apprenticeship: he earns a wage while learning the trade.

exercises.hint: You must learn the trade before you can run a business in it.
exercises.explain: Finish school, do an apprenticeship, qualify, then perhaps start a business.

exercises.prompt: What are values, when choosing a career?
exercises.hint: Values are about what you believe is important.
choices: what matters to you, such as helping people
exercises.explain: What matters most to you, such as helping people, being creative or protecting nature.

exercises.prompt: An apprentice earns 400 gold a month. How much is that in a year?
